html:
Angkor Wat is the temple complex at Angkor, in Cambodia, built in the first half of the 12th century for King Suryavarman II of the Khmer Empire. It is the largest religious monument in the world.

It was built as a Hindu temple to Vishnu, and probably as the king's tomb, which may be why it faces west, the direction linked with death. Its plan is a model of the universe. The five central towers stand for the peaks of Mount Meru, home of the gods, the walls for the mountains at the edge of the world, and the wide moat for the ocean.

What makes it remarkable:

  • Its size: the site covers about 1.6 square kilometres.
  • Its carved galleries, with bas-reliefs running for hundreds of metres, showing the Churning of the Ocean of Milk, scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata, and the king's army on the march.
  • Its unity: the whole was planned and built in one style within a few decades.

From the late 13th century, as Khmer kings turned to Buddhism, it became a Buddhist temple. Unlike most temples at Angkor it was never abandoned, and monks have used it ever since. Later Buddhist builders, starting with Jayavarman VII at the nearby Bayon, followed its example.

Western visitors brought it world fame in the 19th century, especially the French naturalist Henri Mouhot in the 1860s. It appears on the flag of Cambodia, and it is a match in ambition for Java's Borobudur, built three centuries earlier.
sum: Angkor Wat is the temple complex at Angkor, in Cambodia, built in the first half of the 12th century for King Suryavarman II of the Khmer Empire. It is the largest religious monument in the world.
